planting.note: Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost and transplant into warm soil once nights stay above 60F, since this pepper sulks in cool conditions.

directions: Xcatik ('blonde' in Yucatec Maya) is a slender, pale yellow-green chile that ripens to orange, with mild-to-moderate heat similar to a güero pepper. It is the traditional chile of Yucatán, roasted and ground into the seasoning paste for relleno negro and sikil pak, or pickled whole alongside pork dishes. Grow it like other long-season Capsicum annuum peppers in full sun with consistent moisture and a layer of mulch to buffer root temperature, and expect steady fruit set through a long, humid summer.
sources: Seed Savers Exchange heirloom pepper listings

planting.note: Direct-sow once soil is thoroughly warm, as this cowpea landrace germinates fastest above 75F and resents cold, wet soil.

directions: Xpelón is a small, dark-seeded cowpea landrace grown throughout the Yucatán Peninsula, where the tender young pods and shelled green seeds are stewed into the classic potaje de xpelón and the dried beans flavor frijol con puerco. It is a short, bushy, drought-tolerant type bred for the shallow, rocky limestone soils of the region, so it needs little irrigation once established and tolerates heat better than most temperate cowpeas. Harvest some pods young and green for fresh eating and let the rest dry fully on the plant for storage beans.

planting.note: Start seed indoors well ahead of the last frost since germination is slow and erratic, then harden off and transplant only after nights are reliably warm.

directions: Ulupica is a pea-sized, intensely pungent wild chile gathered and semi-cultivated in the dry valleys around Cochabamba and Tarija in Bolivia, where it grows as a shrubby perennial often treated as an annual in cultivation. The tiny berries are traditionally dried and ground into a fiery condiment or crushed fresh into sauces for stews and roasted meats. It prefers lean, well-drained soil and minimal watering, mimicking the rocky scrubland habitat it grows wild in, and is slower to establish than common garden peppers.

planting.note: Plant grafted or container-grown transplants in spring in a sheltered, sunny spot with well-drained soil, since young trees need a few frost-free seasons to establish before heavy fruiting begins.

directions: Capulí is the highland cherry of Ecuador and the northern Andes, bearing small, dark, slightly tart-sweet fruit on a vigorous tree adapted to cool, high-elevation valleys rather than lowland tropics. Fruit is eaten fresh out of hand, stewed into compotes, or used in jams and the fermented chicha de capulí traditional to Andean festivals. Trees tolerate poor soils and light frost once mature but benefit from regular watering during fruit set, and pruning to an open center improves fruit size and airflow in humid highland climates.
sources: INIAP (Ecuadorian national agricultural research institute) fruit tree records

planting.note: Plant small whole seed tubers a few weeks before the last frost in loose, fertile soil, since this short-season diploid potato matures faster than standard tetraploid varieties.

directions: Papa criolla is a small, round, deep-yellow-fleshed potato from the Colombian Andes, botanically a diploid Phureja-group potato distinct from the common tetraploid potato grown elsewhere. It is the defining ingredient of ajiaco bogotano, where it breaks down to thicken the soup, and is also fried whole as a crisp snack. The plants are shorter and quicker to mature than standard potatoes, preferring the cool, bright days and cool nights of high-altitude growing conditions, and tubers are harvested small rather than left to bulk up.
sources: CIP (International Potato Center) Solanum Phureja germplasm records

planting.note: Transplant rooted vines after frost danger has passed next to a sturdy trellis, since gulupa is a vigorous climber that needs support and good airflow to fruit well.

directions: Gulupa is a smooth-skinned, deep-purple passionfruit cultivated in the cool high-altitude valleys of the Colombian Andes, where the climate gives it a sweeter, less acidic pulp than lowland purple or yellow passionfruit types. Vines need a strong trellis or arbor, regular feeding, and consistent moisture through flowering and fruit set, but unlike many passionfruit they tolerate cooler nights without dropping flowers. The jelly-like pulp and crunchy seeds are scooped straight from the halved fruit, blended into juices, or used in desserts, and Colombia exports gulupa internationally as a specialty fruit distinct from common passionfruit.
sources: FAO Colombian horticultural export crop profiles
